text: Pushed the pram onto the grass, my daughter sat on the stone canopy step, and my son slept on me for an hour in the shade. Nobody else was using it. It is the free answer to I need somewhere flat and quiet for an hour, and the only catch is there are no toilets.

Benches in the shade, flat grass, and a canopy to sit under when it rains. I have used this as a waiting place for twenty years. No public toilet, which in this district is normal but never convenient.

Six steps and two flights, and then a room with an enormous shaft overhead and belts you can walk right up to. Both of my children were more interested in this than in any museum we have been to. Free, and almost nobody else there.
The room I most wanted to see is up two flights and I could only manage the ground floor, which is a corridor and a panel. I am annoyed on my own behalf because the toilets up there are good.

We went on a Monday evening because the description says the whole crowd is at Juhu, and it was. Twelve people on the stone edge, the bandstand, and a sunset. Flat the whole promenade, benches, and the horse rides at the far end if you have a child who wants one.
Flat promenade and good with a pram, and then the sand, which is a soft slope you cannot push a stroller up. We sat on the stone edge and had ice cream instead. No toilets, so plan that.

Small shrine, ten minutes round it, and the sea on three sides. The steps down to the water are steep and uneven and I would not attempt them, but the shrine itself is flat once you are up. It is right at Chowpatty so it costs nothing extra.
We got a good ten minutes on the level bit and the pram would not go down the steps to the sea, which is what my son wanted. Flat to the shrine, then a wall.

Flat concrete the whole way, a proper sea breeze, and about a tenth of the people on Marine Drive. We walked half an hour and had shade at one end. The sand is unusable, so the seawall is the whole thing.
Great for the wind and the view of the towers behind you, and there is a long stretch with nothing on it at all, which is either the point or the problem depending on your day. No toilets anywhere.

An old tank in a lane of houses, people bathing at seven in the morning, and nobody filming anything. Ten minutes sitting on the steps. The access is steps on every side, so it is honestly not for a stroller or a walking frame.
I should have read the accessibility note. It is steps, and steep, wet steps, and we stood on the lane above looking down at it. There is nothing to do from up there.
signalTags: nothing to see from the lane

text: A painter who has done rickshaws for thirty years taught my two to do a border and a small motif on a piece of canopy. They took it home and put it on the wall. The bench is against a wall on a steep road, so getting there is the hard part for anyone with a bad knee.

The painting needed no mobility at all and I would have been happy. The climb up Malabar Hill in a hired auto was the problem and we took three tries to get a car up there. Ask for the auto to drop you at the top instead.

A concrete terrace on a residential road with the whole western skyline below it and about four other people there. Half hour, free, no vendors. Stepped lane from the road, so I would not send anybody who cannot manage steps.
The lane up is stepped and steep and I could not do it. We got there by taxi and then still could not find the terrace entrance, which is not signed at all. Wasted a taxi and an hour.

Flat wall, wide walkway, a mosque at one end, and a genuinely cool breeze. No sand you can sit on and the sea is dangerous, so everybody stays on the wall, which is fine. The link between Bandra and Juhu, so it fills a gap in a walk rather than being a destination.
signalTags: fills a gap in a walk

text: Flat all the way with benches, which is what we wanted, but the wind picked up and my husband had to turn back after twenty minutes. The sea there is not for standing near. No toilets.

Good bread, a courtyard, and a front room that is level. My husband sat in the front room and I went out to the courtyard, which has two steps. There is no toilet, which is a shame for a place you sit in for an hour.
Pleasant and civilised and the courtyard was full so we were on the pavement with our coffee watching scooters, which was not what any of us wanted. Get there at one rather than half past.

At seven in the morning the beach is ours and it is enormous, with a flat paved promenade above it. By four in the afternoon the same beach is unmanageable with children. Same beach, completely different problem, and it is a ninety minute visit if you want to walk the whole thing.

Sunset is the whole reason people come and it is worth it once. The promenade is flat, wide and full, and getting onto the sand is a soft slope so plan to stay up. No public toilets on the beach that I could find.

Got there at nine and had room to walk. Textiles, baskets, a wall of chillies, and a food section at the end. Wide aisles and level ground, so the pram was fine, and my daughter bought a basket she did not need.
Came at half past twelve and the last tables were packing up, so the market is really a morning thing. Bought chillies and a dhoti, both good, and there are no toilets which is the thing to know.

Biryani, kheema and kulfi at a junction at nine at night for about two hundred and fifty rupees each, and it is a working neighbourhood rather than a scene. Benches on the mosque side. The kulfi afterwards is the correct decision.

Loud, hot, and there is nowhere to sit except a bench on the mosque side that people had already claimed. The food was very good and we stood for forty minutes. It is a young place, not an old one, and the description should be blunter.

Six of us including three children, a large table, a proper high chair, and a menu that is entirely vegetarian and genuinely good. Nobody asked us to split up, nothing was too loud, and the room has a toilet on the same floor. This is the family restaurant the rest of the area should be reading about.
Step-free, level, a toilet on the same floor, and they did not mind us taking an hour. Lunch is the better sitting than dinner because the room is calmer and the light is better.

Enormous flat green with stables and mature trees, and my son ran for an hour. It is closed on racing days and nobody tells you the calendar, so we nearly wasted a morning. It is a very long walk from anywhere in Colaba or Fort, which is the real problem.

We set out from a Colaba hotel with ninety minutes and made it a third of the way. The place is fine, the distance is the whole story, and anyone planning this from the Fort should be told in kilometres before they commit.

Two rooms of somebody's actual house, opened on a Saturday by a member of the family, with original plasterwork and a verandah. A narrow hall, stairs at the gate, and I would not send a wheelchair. An hour of being shown round by somebody who lives there.

Flat concrete, the creek, the fishing boats and the skyline in one line, and not one other person. Free, twenty-five minutes, and the traffic overhead is the only downside. It is the reason to take the long side of Worli rather than the fast one.
Flat and level, which is good, and my husband sat on the edge wall comfortably. The noise from the road overhead is constant and there is nothing to get a drink, so we did twenty minutes. No toilet.

Water tanks, wooden staircases, washing lines and temple backs, all on flat ground, all in lanes that are empty. We pushed the pram through six lanes without lifting it once. This is the Fort I would rather show people than the frontage.

Worth finding and genuinely different, though a lot of the lanes look like a service road, so it needs twenty minutes of walking before it clicks. Two of the six sections have steps at the far end that the route does not flag.

Lift to every floor, a toilet on each level, wide corridors, benches, and a hearing loop at the desk that the staff explained without being asked. The scale models of the city as it grew are the reason to go and they are better than I expected. It was raining and this was the entire plan.
My ten year old spent forty minutes on the old photographs and ten minutes on the street signs, which is roughly the right ratio. Closed Wednesdays, which caught us once. Cool inside and a dry hour.
signalTags: good with a ten year old

text: Lanterns strung along the wall, carts out, and the shrine lit up. Flat and free to walk, and about as crowded as this city gets. We did it in October, which is when the lanterns are actually out, and it is nothing like the lane in February.

Shoulder to shoulder with nowhere to sit, and I could not keep up with my wife in the crowd. There is a food shop on the same lane that is quiet and does the same job. Do not send an older person who finds crowds difficult into this lane after eight.
